title: Here's What a $5,000 Investment in AMD Could Be Worth by 2032
detail:
Here's What a $5,000 Investment in AMD Could Be Worth by 2032

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) stock has been a standout performer on the market in 2026, with shares of the company rising by an impressive 147% as of this writing, well above the 57% gains clocked by the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index this year.

The impressive rally in AMD stock has been driven by the healthy demand for the company's server central processing units (CPUs) and graphics cards, which are deployed in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Moreover, the company has been doing well in the personal computer (PC) market, even though the industry has been under severe pressure due to high component costs.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But are AMD's catalysts and opportunities strong enough to send the stock soaring over the long run? We will closely examine AMD's growth drivers and see if it is worth investing $5,000 in this semiconductor stock through 2032.

Image source: AMD.
AMD has diversified catalysts that could fuel its growth over the next six years

AMD currently gets the majority of its revenue from the data center segment. In Q2, the data center segment produced 58% of AMD's top line. The segment's revenue increased by 107% year over year to $6.7 billion, which isn't surprising as the company is seeing strong demand for its AI chips.

So, the data center business will play a central role in dictating where AMD stock could be in 2032. The good news for AMD investors is that it expects AI chip demand to remain solid through the end of the decade. Management noted on AMD's recent earnings call that the total addressable market (TAM) for AI data center accelerators is poised to grow at a 45% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) through 2030, generating $1.4 trillion in revenue by the end of the decade.

AMD is well-positioned to capitalize on this lucrative opportunity. That's because the company sells server CPUs, graphics processing units (GPUs), and server rack systems, all of which are in solid demand to handle AI workloads in data centers. Importantly, AMD has been building a solid client base in AI chips.

AMD's server CPUs are being used by major hyperscalers, including Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Google, and others. Additionally, the company's rack-scale server systems, which integrate its GPUs, server CPUs, and networking chips into a single platform, will start shipping in the current quarter. AMD expects "very strong customer demand" for Helios in 2027, and the company's focus on improving the efficiency of its rack-scale systems every year should help it attract more customers.

title: AMD vs. TSMC: How Much Faster Must AMD’s Cash Flow Grow?

Our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade includes both the chip designer and the foundry. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) offers processor and accelerator upside. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) offers exposure to manufacturing many customers' designs. Their starting cash prices set very different hurdles.

AMD vs. TSMC: How Much Faster Must AMD's Cash Flow Grow?

Photo by Christian Wiediger on Unsplash

The starting multiple matters

At October 16 prices, AMD's $863.17 billion equity value compared with $8.40 billion of trailing operating cash after capital expenditure: roughly 103 times. TSMC's comparable cash figure was $45.53 billion. Applying its $412.61 depositary-share price to 25.93 billion ordinary shares, with five ordinary shares per depositary share, gives a U.S.-price-implied equity value near $2.14 trillion and a multiple near 47.

That depositary-share adjustment matters. Mixing ordinary shares with the U.S. trading price would inflate capitalization fivefold. Even correctly calculated multiples are historical snapshots: investment spending, working capital and currency translation can change the denominator.

AMD's growth opportunity is substantial. Second-quarter data-center revenue reached $6.72 billion, more than double a year earlier. Its challenge is turning broader adoption into cash after engineering and investment costs. Our Nvidia-AMD margin analysis tests how much room AMD currently has for pricing disappointment.

A common ending multiple exposes the hurdle

Suppose TSMC's cash flow grows 10% annually for ten years. At unchanged share prices and share counts, AMD would need about 19% annual growth to reach the same ending cash-flow multiple. The calculation compounds the starting multiple gap over ten years; it does not assume either stock actually delivers those returns.

If TSMC's cash growth is zero, AMD's catch-up hurdle is about 8% annually. If TSMC grows 15%, AMD needs about 24%. These are scenarios, not company guidance or justified growth forecasts. AMD could deserve a different ending multiple, and dilution would make the required company-wide growth higher for a given per-share result.

TSMC also has to earn its cash. New fabrication capacity can consume funds long before it produces revenue, while utilization and geographic disruption can undermine returns.

The investment test

Geography also changes the return investors may require.

title: Nvidia vs. AMD: Who Can Afford the Next Jump in Research Spending?
detail:
Nvidia vs. AMD: Who Can Afford the Next Jump in Research Spending?
Habib Ur Rehman
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 1:56 PM CDT 3 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade weighs the ability to keep investing through technology changes. Nvidia and AMD illustrate why the size of a research budget matters less than the business supporting it. Which can absorb another spending increase without sacrificing much of today's profit?

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) spent $7.05 billion on research and development in its quarter ended July 26. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) spent $2.53 billion in its quarter ended June 27.

Nvidia vs. AMD: Who Can Afford the Next Jump in Research Spending?

Courtesy of NVIDIA

A larger budget can be a lighter burden

Research absorbed 7.3% of Nvidia's $96.22 billion revenue and 21.9% of AMD's $11.54 billion. Across their respective first halves, the proportions were 7.5% and 22.6%, so the difference extends beyond one quarter.

Nvidia's advantage is scale: a much larger sales base supports more absolute development spending while leaving substantial operating profit. Its software and systems business can help distribute engineering costs across customers. That does not establish that each research dollar produces a better chip or a stronger investment return.

AMD's higher burden also represents an opportunity. Successful processor and accelerator adoption could spread existing development expense over more revenue. Cutting research simply to improve the ratio could undermine that opportunity. Our margin-resilience comparison shows how differently the two current profit bases respond when pricing pressure arrives instead.

What another 20% would cost

Hold revenue and every other cost fixed, then increase quarterly research spending 20%. Nvidia would absorb another $1.41 billion, reducing its $63.73 billion operating income by 2.2%. AMD would absorb $506 million, reducing its $1.99 billion operating income by 25.4%. This is an expense sensitivity, not guidance: successful research can create future revenue, and actual expenses would not all stay fixed.

At unchanged research spending, AMD would need revenue of $16.85 billion to reduce its research burden to 15%, about 46% above the latest quarter.

Research capacity is not a stock-price verdict

At October 16 equity values, trailing operating cash less capital expenditure cost about 41 times for Nvidia and 103 times for AMD. Neither spending capacity nor a high research ratio settles whether those prices are justified. Our Nvidia-Broadcom investment comparison examines how a different AI-chip business model changes the growth-versus-price decision.

Why AMD Stock Popped on Monday

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock jumped 3.6% through 12:30 p.m. ET Monday.

You can thank the friendly analysts at TD Cowen for that. AMD stock may have lost 16% of its value over the past two weeks as semiconductor stocks sold off, but Cowen still thinks AMD stock is a buy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Why Cowen loves AMD stock

TD Cowen analyst Joshua Buchalter reiterated his buy rating and $675 price target on AMD this morning, citing "growing adoption of agentic AI and production inference workloads." Whereas AI training requires GPUs, you see, AMD's CPUs are better suited for "coordination of multi-step workflows, tool calls, API management, and sequential decision-making" in agentic AI.

AMD seems to agree. The company recently doubled the estimated size of its total addressable market to $220 billion and predicted its sales of CPUs for AI data centers will rise 70% in 2027.

What's next for AMD stock

Is that enough to make AMD stock a buy?

At first glance, the stock still looks richly priced at more than 156 times trailing earnings. But here's the thing: That P/E ratio is based on AMD's $6.4 billion in reported net income. When valued on free cash flow, though, AMD is actually generating more than $8.4 billion in real cash profit.

And that's enough to drop the company's price-to-free cash flow ratio down to just 102x.

Mind you, a P/FCF ratio of 102x still is not obviously "cheap," but with a long-term forecast growth rate of 60%, the stock's price-to-FCF-to-growth ratio is only about 1.7 -- a lot cheap-er than its PEG ratio of 2.6.

While not an obvious bargain, AMD stock is at least a bit cheaper than it looks. While I hesitate to buy it myself, I see why Cowen might think it's a buy.

title: What Just Happened To Marvell Stock?
detail:
What Just Happened To Marvell Stock?
Trefis Team

MRVL
^GSPC
AMD
NVDA
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shares of Marvell Technology (MRVL) fell 17.2% over the five trading days from October 9 to October 16, 2026. The broader market saw far less movement during that window, with the S&P 500 losing 1.9%. The stock first slipped the day after its October 6 Investor Day, an event where management actually raised its revenue outlook for fiscal 2028. So how hard was the week for Marvell, and what does its price still appear to assume?

Marvell's Worst Day Came On October 14

The steepest drop for Marvell occurred on October 14, when shares lost 8.7% in a single session. Other chip stocks also had a weak week over those same dates. Advanced Micro Devices went down 13.0% and NVIDIA fell 6.6%, yet Marvell experienced a deeper decline than both. Earlier in the month, the stock had risen 5.8% on the day of the Investor Day. Ultimately, the week's fall more than erased that gain.

What Marvell's Price Still Appears To Assume

Even after taking this hit, Marvell commanded a steep premium at the October 16 close. The stock traded at 77.4 times its earnings over the past twelve months, well above the 22.9 multiple for the S&P 500. Valuations at that level appear to assume growth far beyond today's results, and management has explicitly put a number on that growth. Executives used the Investor Day to raise the fiscal 2028 revenue outlook to about $20 billion, up from about $18 billion provided during the August 27 earnings call. They also set a fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion.

For context, Marvell generated $9.45 billion in revenue over the past twelve months. Meeting the new outlook will require the company to more than double those sales by fiscal 2028.

Marvell's Latest Results Stand Where They Were

The company reported no new financial results during the week, leaving its latest quarter exactly as it looked before the stock fell. In fiscal Q2 2027, the quarter ended August 1, 2026, Marvell posted revenue of $2.74 billion, a 36.5% increase from a year earlier. The chip designer also kept more of each sale as profit. Its operating margin came in at 16.7%, up from 14.9% a year earlier. Data center served as the largest end market, making up 79% of total revenue according to management on the August 27 call. On the liquidity side, free cash flow over the past twelve months reached $1.72 billion, rising from $1.53 billion a year earlier.

Looking ahead to fiscal Q3 2027, management guided to revenue of $3.15 billion, plus or minus 5%. How actual revenue stacks up against that guide is the number to watch at Marvell's next report, expected on or around November 30, 2026.
